pages.title: Welcome to Lilo
pages.summary: What Lilo does, who it is for, and how to use this guide.
pages.body:
# Welcome to Lilo

Lilo turns a picture, a word or your own drawing into **stitches**, the tiny thread moves an embroidery machine sews. Then it sends the design to your machine.

Say you want your logo on the inside of a suit jacket. You open Lilo, drop in the logo, press one button and watch it sew itself on screen. Then you send it to the machine over Wi-Fi.

You do not need an account. Lilo does not upload your designs anywhere.

## What you can make

- A **picture** stitched from a logo or sketch. Read [Turn a picture into stitches](auto-digitize.md).
- A **monogram**, like "JK" on a suit lining. Read [Lettering](lettering-fonts.md).
- A **crest** or patch drawn from scratch. Read [Drawing tools](drawing-tools.md).
- **Pixel art** in a cross-stitch style. Read [Pixel art](pixel-art.md).
- A **converted file**. Read [The converter](converter.md).

## How this guide works

- **New here?** Start with [Your first design in five minutes](first-design.md).
- **Stuck on a button?** Look for the small round **?** next to it. It tells you what the control does, when to change it and a typical value. It also links to the full page.
- **Looking for something?** Open Help with the **Help** button at the top, or press **⌘?** (**Ctrl+?** on Windows and Linux). Type a word and the pages filter as you type.
- **Something sewed badly?** Go to [Fixing sew-out problems](sewout-troubleshooting.md).

## Four helpers inside the app

- The **workflow strip** at the top of the editor shows five steps and ticks them off for you. Read [Helpers inside Lilo](learning-aids.md).
- The **tour** walks you through your first design. You can replay it from Help.
- **Hints** are the **?** buttons.
- The **warnings tray** tells you, calmly, when something might sew badly, and offers a fix.

## Words you do not know

Embroidery has its own words. Each one is explained the first time it appears. You can also look any word up in the [Glossary](glossary.md).

pages.title: Install Lilo on Mac, Windows or Linux
pages.summary: Download Lilo, open it the first time, and get past the Windows SmartScreen and Linux AppImage prompts.
pages.body:
# Install Lilo on Mac, Windows or Linux

Get the newest version from the **Releases page** on the Lilo GitHub project (github.com/Kadwood/lilo/releases/latest). Every release has a `SHA256SUMS` file. It lets you check that your download was not changed on the way.

## Mac

You need macOS 13 or newer. Apple Silicon and Intel Macs both work.

1. Download `Lilo_<version>_universal.dmg`.
2. Open it and drag **Lilo** onto **Applications**.
3. Open Lilo. Lilo is signed and notarized by Apple. The first time, macOS says it was downloaded from the internet. Click **Open**.
4. The first time you look for machines on your network, macOS asks to allow **Local Network** access. Say yes. Without it Lilo cannot find your sewing machine.

## Windows

You need 64-bit Windows.

1. Download `Lilo_<version>_x64-setup.exe` and run it.
2. Windows may show a blue box that says **Windows protected your PC**. That is SmartScreen. It appears because the Lilo installer is not code-signed yet. It does not mean the file is bad.
3. Click **More info**, then **Run anyway**.

The installer works for your user only. You do not need admin rights.

## Linux

You need 64-bit Linux. Pick one file.

- **AppImage:** download `Lilo_<version>_amd64.AppImage`. Make it runnable with `chmod +x Lilo_*.AppImage`, then double-click it or run it from a terminal. On newer Ubuntu you also need FUSE 2. Install it with `sudo apt install libfuse2`.
- **Deb package:** download `Lilo_<version>_amd64.deb` and run `sudo apt install ./Lilo_*.deb`.

## Updates

Lilo checks the Releases page once a day when it starts. If there is a new version, a banner offers **Install and restart**. Lilo only talks to that page. You can turn the check off, or run it by hand, under **Lilo Link**, then **Settings**, then **Updates**.

## Next step

Open Lilo and follow [Your first design in five minutes](first-design.md).

# Your first design in five minutes

You will turn a logo into stitches. Use any simple picture with flat colours, like the Kadwood hibiscus.

![The Home screen with the six starting cards](screenshots/home-start.png)

## 1. Get a design

1. On **Home**, click **Digitize a picture…**.
2. Choose a PNG, JPG, WEBP or SVG file.
3. Watch Lilo trace the picture and lay stitches on screen. This takes a few seconds.

**Digitize** means "turn a picture into stitches". Lilo does it for you.

## 2. Size it and pick a hoop

The **hoop** is the frame that holds the cloth tight. Your design must fit inside it.

1. In the left panel, set **Width** in millimetres. A logo on a suit lining often works at 40 to 80 mm.
2. Check the **hoop** chip. If your design sticks out of the frame, press **Smallest hoop that fits**, or choose your machine's hoop. Read [Sizing and hoops](sizing-and-hoops.md).

## 3. Tell Lilo what you are sewing on

Open the **Sewing setup** card on the right. Pick the **fabric**, the **thread weight** and the **quality**. Lilo adjusts spacing and underlay for you. Read [Sewing setup](sewing-setup.md).

## 4. Preview

Press **Play** in the stitch player under the canvas. The needle sews the design stitch by stitch. It stops at each colour change and tells you which thread to swap in.

## 5. Send or export

- Press **Send** to send it to a Brother or Baby Lock machine over Wi-Fi. Read [Send a design](send-a-design.md).
- Press **Export** to save a file for a USB stick or another machine. Read [Choosing a format](export-formats.md).

## Watch the workflow strip

The strip at the top of the editor has five steps: **Get a design**, **Size and hoop**, **Stitches**, **Preview** and **Send**. Each ticks itself off when you finish it. Click a step to open the right panel and see a tip.

## Before you sew for real

Always sew a test on a scrap of the same cloth. Lilo's numbers are good starting points, not promises. If the test puckers or leaves gaps, go to [Fixing sew-out problems](sewout-troubleshooting.md).

pages.body:
# The screen at a glance

![The editor with each area numbered](screenshots/editor-overview.png)

The editor has the same layout every time. Here is where things live.

## Top of the window

- **Views** (Home, Editor, Pixel art, Converter, Lilo Link) switch between the parts of the app. **Help** opens this guide.
- The **top bar** holds the project menu, the project name, the **hoop** chooser, a search box (**⌘K**), **Export** and **Send**.
- The **workflow strip** shows your five steps. Read [Helpers inside Lilo](learning-aids.md).

## Left panel

This panel changes with what you have selected.

- **Nothing selected:** **Auto-digitize** settings and the hoop.
- **A shape selected:** its size, colour, stitch type and fill settings.
- **Text tool or a word selected:** the lettering panel.
- **Click to stitch tool:** the regions panel.

## The canvas

The big middle area. It shows your hoop, a grid and your design. Zoom with scroll or pinch. Pan by holding **Space** and dragging. The small checkboxes in the corner switch the **Realistic**, **Grid**, **Reference** and **Jumps** views.

When you select a shape, a small **shape bar** floats above it with actions like **Reshape**, **Cut hole**, **Knife** and **Duplicate**.

## The toolbar

The floating bar at the bottom holds the drawing tools, **Undo**, **Redo** and your **drawing colour**. Read [Drawing tools](drawing-tools.md).

## The stitch player

Under the canvas. **Play**, scrub and change the speed. It also shows the totals: stitches, size, colour changes and sewing time. Read [The stitch player](stitch-player.md).

## Right column

- **Sewing setup:** fabric, thread weight and quality. Read [Sewing setup](sewing-setup.md).
- **Sequencer:** the order your shapes are sewn in. It has tabs for objects, colours, images and your threads. Read [The sequencer](sequencer.md).

## The warnings tray

When Lilo spots something that may sew badly, a small tray appears in the right-hand column, under the Sewing setup card. It is calm and never blocks you. Read [What the warnings mean](warnings-explained.md).

pages.title: Embroidery basics: stabiliser, hoop, thread and bobbin
pages.summary: The four physical things every sew-out needs, explained from scratch.
pages.body:
# Embroidery basics: stabiliser, hoop, thread and bobbin

An embroidery machine does not move the cloth like a normal sewing machine. It holds the cloth still in a frame and moves the frame under the needle. These four things make that work.

## Stabiliser

**Stabiliser** is a sheet of backing you put under the cloth. Think of it as the paper you draw on when you do not want a thin page to crumple. Thousands of stitches pull on cloth. Without a backing, the cloth bunches up around the design.

- **Cut-away** stays in the garment. You trim around the design. It is the safe choice for stretchy cloth and anything you wash a lot.
- **Tear-away** rips off after sewing. It suits stable, tightly woven cloth.
- **No-show mesh** is a soft cut-away for thin cloth like a shirt or a suit lining. It does not scratch and does not show through.
- **Water-soluble topping** sits on top of fluffy cloth like towel, so stitches do not sink into the pile.

The **Sewing setup** card tells you which type fits your fabric. Read [Sewing setup presets](sewing-presets.md).

## Hoop

The **hoop** is the frame that holds cloth and stabiliser flat and tight. It has two rings. You press the cloth between them and tighten a screw.

The machine can only sew inside the hoop. Every hoop has a **sewing area**, a little smaller than the frame itself. Lilo draws that area on the canvas and warns you if your design sticks out. Read [Sizing and hoops](sizing-and-hoops.md).

A good hoop job feels like a drum. The cloth is tight but not stretched. Stretched cloth springs back after sewing and puckers the design.

## Thread

The **top thread** is what you see. Most embroidery uses **40 wt** thread. The "wt" number says how thin it is. A bigger number means thinner thread. **60 wt** is finer. It lets you sew smaller, crisper details, like tiny letters.

Thread comes in **brands** and each brand has its own colour codes. Lilo knows many. Read [Thread brands and matching](thread-brands-matching.md).

## Bobbin

The **bobbin** is a small spool of thread under the needle plate. It makes the back of the stitch. Embroidery bobbin thread is usually thinner and often white or black.

A good sew-out shows only a little bobbin thread on the front. If you see a lot of bobbin thread, the top thread is too tight. Read [Fixing sew-out problems](sewout-troubleshooting.md).

## Needle

Use a fresh needle. A dull needle shreds thread and punches holes. Lilo's Sewing setup suggests a size for your fabric and thread, like **75/11** for most cloth or **70/10** for a thin lining.

## Next step

Read [Stitch terms: density, pull compensation and underlay](basics-stitch-terms.md).

pages.title: Stitch terms: density, pull compensation and underlay
pages.summary: Three ideas that decide whether a design looks crisp or messy, with a picture of each.
pages.body:
# Stitch terms: density, pull compensation and underlay

Three ideas explain most of the settings in Lilo.

## Density

**Density** is how close the stitches sit to each other. Closer stitches cover the cloth better. Too close, and the needle punches so many holes that the cloth tears or the thread snaps.

Lilo measures density as a gap in millimetres. **Smaller gap means denser.** For satin columns with 40 wt thread, 0.40 mm is the usual starting point. Read [Satin tips](satin-tips.md).

## Pull compensation

Thread pulls cloth inward as it tightens. A stitched circle ends up a little smaller and narrower than you drew it. **Pull compensation** makes each shape a little bigger on purpose, so it ends up the right size after the pull.

![A satin column drawn at 4 mm, pulled in by the thread, then widened by pull compensation](diagrams/pull-compensation.svg)

Stretchy cloth pulls more, so it needs more compensation. Lilo's **Sewing setup** adds extra for knits. Read [Underlay and pull compensation](underlay-and-pull.md).

## Underlay

**Underlay** is a layer of light stitches sewn first, under the pretty stitches. It does two jobs. It holds the cloth to the stabiliser. And it gives the top stitches something to sit on, so they look raised and even.

![Cross-section showing cloth, stabiliser, underlay and top stitches](diagrams/underlay-layers.svg)

You will not see underlay in a good sew-out. You will notice when it is missing: the design looks flat and thin and the cloth shows through.

## Satin and fill

Lilo uses two main stitch types for areas.

- **Satin** is a column of side-to-side stitches. It looks shiny and smooth. It suits letters and borders from about 1.5 to 8 mm wide.
- **Fill** is rows of stitches that cover a large area. It suits big shapes.

![Satin column next to a fill area](diagrams/satin-vs-fill.svg)

Read [Run stitches versus fills](run-vs-fill.md).

pages.body:
# Helpers inside Lilo: tour, strip, hints and warnings

Lilo has four helpers. All of them are quiet. None of them stops you from working.

## The first-launch tour

The first time you open Lilo, a friendly host asks what you want to make:

- a **picture**,
- a drawing **from scratch**,
- a **monogram**, or
- an **existing file**.

Each choice shows a few short tips that point at the real buttons. A tip moves on when you do the thing it asks, so you learn by doing. You can **Skip** at any time. Lilo remembers that you finished or skipped, and does not show it again.

To see it again, open **Help** and press **Replay the tour**.

## The workflow strip

Five steps sit across the top of the editor.

1. **Get a design** ticks when the canvas has something on it.
2. **Size and hoop** ticks when the design fits the hoop.
3. **Stitches** ticks when Lilo sees no stitch quality problems.
4. **Preview** ticks when you have played the stitches or looked at the realistic view.
5. **Send** ticks when you have exported or sent the design.

Click any step. The panel for that step opens and a small tip card explains what to do.

## Hints

A small round **?** sits next to almost every control. Click it, or tab to it and press Enter. A card shows:

- **What it does** in a few words,
- **When to change it**,
- a **typical value**, and
- a **Read more** link to the full guide page.

Press **Esc** to close it.

## The warnings tray

When Lilo spots something that may sew badly, a note appears in a small tray in the right-hand column, under the Sewing setup card. For example: your design is bigger than the hoop, or your letters are too small for the thread. Each note has a button that fixes it in one click, or a link to read more. You can dismiss a note. It stays dismissed until the problem changes.

Read [What the warnings mean](warnings-explained.md).

## Opening Help from anywhere

- Click **Help** at the top of the window.
- Press **⌘?** on Mac or **Ctrl+?** on Windows and Linux.
- Click any **?** and then **Read more**.

pages.summary: Open a logo or sketch and let Lilo trace it, pick thread colours and lay stitches.
pages.body:
# Turn a picture into stitches

**Digitizing** means turning a picture into stitch instructions. Lilo can do the whole thing in one go. This is called **Auto digitize**.

## Open a picture

Use **Digitize a picture…** on Home, or **Open image…** in the left panel. You can also drop a PNG, JPG, WEBP or SVG file onto the canvas.

Flat, high-contrast pictures work best: a logo, a crest, a simple drawing. Photos with soft shading make messy embroidery, because thread cannot blend like pixels do.

## The settings, top to bottom

- **Colours** is how many thread colours to use, from 2 to 12. Fewer colours mean fewer thread changes and a faster sew. Start with the number of colours you see.
- **Size (mm)** is the width and height of the finished design. Leave one box on **auto** and Lilo keeps the shape. Small details drop out below about 80 mm for fine serif logos, so size up if the hairlines vanish.
- **Smallest region** drops tiny specks. A region smaller than this many square millimetres is merged away. Raise it if you see dust-like dots.
- **Background** is **Remove** or **Keep**. **Remove** treats the picture's background colour as empty cloth. Choose **Keep** if the background is part of the design.
- **Thread brand** picks the thread range to match against. Read [Thread brands and matching](thread-brands-matching.md).
- **Quality**, **Thread weight** and **Fabric** make up the Sewing setup. Read [Standard or Premium](standard-vs-premium.md).
- **Use my threads** matches colours to the spools you own first. Read [My Threads](my-threads.md).

Press **Digitize** to run it again after you change a setting.

## What Lilo does

1. It shrinks the picture and removes the background.
2. It reduces the picture to your chosen number of colours.
3. It snaps each colour to the nearest real thread.
4. It traces the shapes.
5. It decides how to stitch each shape. Thin lines become a running stitch. Medium shapes become satin columns. Wide shapes become fills with underlay.
6. It orders the shapes so the machine jumps as little as possible.

Everything it makes is editable. Select any shape and change it.

## If the result looks wrong

- **Too many colours:** lower **Colours**.
- **Missing thin lines:** make the design larger, or choose **Premium**, which sews fine strokes as narrow satin.
- **Messy specks:** raise **Smallest region**.
- **Wrong colours:** change the thread in the left panel after selecting a shape, or use the **Colours** tab in the sequencer to merge or swap.

When you want control over which parts get stitched, use [Click to stitch](click-to-stitch.md).

pages.title: Click to stitch
pages.summary: Choose, region by region, which parts of a traced picture get stitched and how.
pages.body:
# Click to stitch

**Auto digitize** decides everything for you. **Click to stitch** hands you the controls. Lilo traces the picture into **regions**, the coloured areas. You click the ones you want.

Use it when you want the crest's border as satin, the fabric background left alone, and only the centre filled.

## Steps

1. Open an image. Lilo traces it.
2. Choose the **Click to stitch** tool (press **K**), or press **Click to stitch…** in the left panel.
3. Pick **fill** or **outline** settings in the panel.
4. Click a region to stitch it.
5. To stitch several regions together, **Shift**-click each one, then press **Enter**.
6. Press **Esc** to leave the tool.

Each click is one undo step. Press **⌘Z** if you do not like it.

## Starting from a bare trace

If you already used **Digitize**, use the panel's clear button to remove all stitches. You then start from the bare trace and stitch only what you pick.

## Tips

- Stitch the biggest regions first, then the details on top.
- Choose **outline** for regions thinner than a few millimetres, where a fill would look heavy.
- You can change a stitched region afterwards. Select it and use the left panel. Read [Editing shapes](editing-shapes.md).

pages.body:
# Drawing tools

The floating toolbar at the bottom of the canvas holds the tools. Press the key to switch tools. Press **⌘K** to search for any tool by name.

![The toolbar with each tool labelled](screenshots/toolbar.png)

## Moving around

- **Select (S).** Click to select a shape. Drag to move it. Drag on empty space to box-select. **Shift** adds to the selection.
- **Pan (Space).** Drag to move the view. Hold **Space** to pan with any tool.
- **Measure (M).** Drag between two points to read the distance in millimetres. Use it to check a crest against a hoop.

## Drawing shapes

- **Open shape (1).** Click to add points. Right-click or double-click for a curve point. **Enter** finishes. **Esc** cancels. Good for a stem or a border line.
- **Closed shape (2).** Like Open shape, but the outline closes into a fill. Click the first point or press **Enter** to close. Good for a leaf or a badge outline.
- **Circle (3).** Drag a box for an ellipse. Hold **Ctrl** for a perfect circle. Good for a round hat patch.
- **Rectangle (4).** Drag a box. Hold **Ctrl** for a square.
- **Pen (5).** Draw freehand. Lilo smooths the line when you let go. Finish near the start to close it.
- **Satin blocks (6).** Click the left edge, then the right edge, and repeat along the column. **Enter** finishes. You control the exact slant of each stitch block. Good for a curved border or a leaf.
- **Manual stitch (7).** Click to place each stitch exactly where you want the needle. **Enter** finishes. Use it for small touch-ups.

## Words and pictures

- **Text (T).** Click where the text goes, then type in the panel. Read [Lettering](lettering-fonts.md).
- **Click to stitch (K).** Read [Click to stitch](click-to-stitch.md).

## The drawing colour

The coloured dot in the toolbar is the thread your **next** shape will use. Select a shape to change its own colour.

## Undo and redo

**⌘Z** undoes the last step. **⇧⌘Z** redoes it. Sliders merge into one undo step, so one **⌘Z** undoes a whole drag.

## A tip for a round patch

For a 50 mm hat patch, draw a **Circle** and set **Style** to **Outlined**. Choose the **Satin** run type with a width of 3 mm for the border. Then add a filled circle inside. Read [Run types](run-types.md).

pages.title: Editing shapes
pages.summary: Reshape, cut holes, slice, set start points, duplicate, lock and map shapes along a path.

headings.text: The left panel for a shape

pages.body:
# Editing shapes

Click a shape and a small **shape bar** floats above it. It has one button per action. Disabled buttons are greyed out because they do not apply to what you selected.

## The shape bar

- **Reshape.** Move, add and delete points. Double-click a point to switch it between a corner and a curve. You can also double-click a shape to start.
- **Cut hole.** Draw a closed shape inside a fill to cut it out. Use it for the hole in the letter "O" or a ring.
- **Knife.** Drag a line across a shape to slice it in two.
- **Start** and **End.** Click on the canvas to choose where sewing starts and ends. A green marker shows the start and a red one the end. A start near other shapes means fewer jumps.
- **Angle.** Turn the stitch direction with a dial on the canvas. Only for fills.
- **Map to path** (**P**). Repeat the selection along an open line. Read below.
- **Outline** or **Fill.** Converts between an outlined shape and a filled one.
- **Redwork.** Adds a running outline along every edge of the selection, routed to keep jumps short.
- **Lock** or **Unlock.** Locks the selection so you cannot move or edit it by accident.
- **Duplicate** (**⌘D**) and **Delete** (**Backspace**).

## The left panel for a shape

With a shape selected, the left panel shows its settings: **Dimensions**, **Colour**, **Style**, then the stitch settings for its type. Read [Run types](run-types.md), [Underlay and pull compensation](underlay-and-pull.md) and [Satin tips](satin-tips.md).

Every change shows on the canvas straight away. Sliders merge into one undo step.

## Several shapes at once

Select more than one shape and the panel edits all of them. The panel shows the settings of the first shape. Change one control and it applies to everyone selected.

## Map to path

**Map to path** places copies of a shape along an open line. Use it for a row of stars along a garment-bag strap crest, or small leaves along a vine.

1. Select the shape and the open line together, then press **P**. Or select the shape, press **P** and choose a path afterwards.
2. Set the **count** and **spacing** in the dialog.
3. Apply it.

The copies stay linked. Use **Edit…** in the **Map to path** section of the left panel to change the count, or **Detach** to turn them into ordinary shapes.

## Reorder and hide

Open the sequencer on the right to change sewing order, hide shapes or group by colour. Read [The sequencer](sequencer.md).

headings.text: Fitting a design that is too big

pages.body:
# Sizing and hoops

A design has to fit inside the **sewing area** of the hoop. This page shows how to set the size and pick the hoop.

![The standard hoop sizes drawn to scale](diagrams/hoop-sizes.svg)

## Set the size

Select a shape (or **⌘A** for everything) and open **Dimensions** in the left panel.

- Type a **Width** or **Height** in millimetres. Switch to inches with the **Units** buttons.
- **Keep aspect ratio** (the padlock) changes width and height together so the shape does not squash. Turn it off to stretch one side.
- Use **Flip left-right**, **Flip top-bottom** and **Rotate 90°** under the size boxes.

The top-left corner stays put when you resize.

Nothing selected? **Auto-digitize** has its own width and height boxes. They set the size of the next result.

## Choose a hoop

The **hoop chip** in the top bar and in the **Hoop** section shows the current hoop. Click it to open the picker.

- Search by **brand**, **machine** or hoop name.
- Recently used hoops come first.
- **Smallest hoop that fits** picks the smallest hoop that holds your design.
- **Swap width and height** rotates the hoop between landscape and portrait.
- **Add my own…** saves a custom hoop with your own width and height.

Lilo ships a library of real hoops. Where a size could not be confirmed it says so. Check the numbers against your own hoop.

## What the frame shows

- The **hoop frame** and its clamp are drawn around the sewing area.
- The **safe margin** is a dashed line 5 mm inside the sewing area. Stitches close to the edge can hit the hoop.
- **Rulers** run along the top and left. Drag from a ruler to pull out a guide line.
- **Placement guides** show where a design usually goes: a left chest, a pocket, the centre of a hat. Pick one from the list.

## See it at real size

**Actual size** (**⌘0**) shows the design at its true size on your screen. Use **Calibrate screen…** once. You hold a ruler to the screen and Lilo learns how big a millimetre is on your display.

## Fitting a design that is too big

If the design sticks out, Lilo shows a warning in the tray. Pick a larger hoop or scale the design down. Do not squeeze a dense design into a small size without checking density. Read [What the warnings mean](warnings-explained.md).

pages.title: Run stitches versus fills
pages.summary: The two families of stitches in Lilo, when to pick each, and how Style switches between them.

headings.text: What is the difference in sewing?

pages.body:
# Run stitches versus fills

Every shape you draw is sewn one of two ways.

- A **run** follows a line. Think of drawing with a pen. It can be a thin single line, a thick satin ribbon or a twisted rope.
- A **fill** covers an area. Think of colouring in with a marker.

![A satin column next to a fill area, with stitch directions marked](diagrams/satin-vs-fill.svg)

## Which one should I use?

| You want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A thin outline or a stem | Run, **Single** or **Triple** |
| A bold border or a letter stroke | Run, **Satin** |
| A big area like a leaf or a badge face | Fill |
| A textured area like a brick wall | Fill with a motif pattern |

## Switching a shape

A closed shape can be either. In the left panel, **Style** has two buttons: **Filled** sews the whole area, **Outlined** sews only the edge using any run type. The shape bar's **Outline** and **Fill** button does the same.

## What is the difference in sewing?

A run is quick and light. A fill is slower and uses many more stitches. A fill of a 40 by 30 mm area can take thousands of stitches. A satin column of the same length uses far fewer.

## Which settings go with which?

- Runs have a **run type**. Read [Run types](run-types.md).
- Satin runs and satin blocks have **density**, **pull compensation** and **underlay**. Read [Satin tips](satin-tips.md).
- Fills have a **pattern**, **row spacing** and their own underlay. Read [All fill patterns](fill-patterns.md) and [Underlay and pull compensation](underlay-and-pull.md).

pages.title: Run types
pages.summary: The seven ways Lilo can sew along a line: single, triple, satin, E-stitch, double rope, triple rope and manual.
pages.body:
# Run types

A **run** follows a line you drew. Lilo has seven ways to sew it. Choose one in **Run type** in the left panel.

## Single

One line of stitches. The everyday **running stitch**. Use it for fine outlines, stems and quilting lines.

- **Stitch length** is the distance between needle drops. 2.5 to 3 mm is typical.
- **Tolerance** is how far a stitch may stray from the curve you drew. Lower follows curves more closely. The minimum is 0.1 mm.

## Triple

Each stitch is sewn forward, back and forward again. The line is heavier and bolder. Also called a **bean stitch**. Use it for outlines that need to stand out, or for thin details that a single line would lose.

## Satin

A column of fixed width along the line, like a pen stroke with thread across it. Set the **Width** in the panel, usually 2 to 6 mm. It also has a **Satin** section for density, pull compensation and underlay. Read [Satin tips](satin-tips.md).

## E-stitch

Comb-shaped stitches that reach out from the line. Use it for appliqué edges and decorative borders. **Width** sets how far the teeth reach. **Flipped** puts the teeth on the other side of the line.

## Double rope

A twisted cord sewn in two passes. Use it for a thin braid border, like piping around a patch. **Width** is how wide the twist is. The default is 0.4 mm.

## Triple rope

A thicker twisted cord from three passes. Use it for a bolder braid.

## Manual

Sews exactly the stitch points you placed with the **Manual stitch** tool, in order. Lilo does not move them. Reshape the shape to move points.

## Changing the type

Select the shape. Click a type. Lilo keeps your length and swaps the other settings to sensible defaults for the new type. Press **⌘Z** to undo.

![Seven run types side by side](screenshots/run-types.png)

headings.text: How to tell if you need more

pages.body:
# Underlay and pull compensation

## Underlay

**Underlay** is the layer of light stitches sewn before the visible ones. Read the idea first in [Stitch terms](basics-stitch-terms.md).

![Cross-section: cloth, stabiliser, underlay, top stitches](diagrams/underlay-layers.svg)

### Satin underlay choices

Pick one from the **Underlay** list in the **Satin** section.

| Choice | What it is | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None | No underlay | Very thin columns, or when you add your own |
| Center run | One line down the middle | Columns under about 2.5 mm |
| Contour | A line right inside each edge | Medium columns |
| Zig-zag | Back-and-forth across the column | Wider columns |
| Contour + zig-zag | Edge walk plus zig-zag | Wide columns on soft cloth |
| Center + contour | Middle line plus edge walk | Columns of about 2.5 to 4 mm |
| Double zig-zag | Two zig-zag passes | Columns wider than about 6 mm |

When Lilo digitizes for you it picks one by width: centre run under 2.5 mm, centre plus edge up to 4 mm, edge plus zig-zag up to 6 mm, and double zig-zag beyond that. You can change it.

### Fill underlay

In the **Underlay** section of a fill:

- The **Underlay** switch adds one light pass at right angles to the fill.
- **Customise underlays…** lets you add several passes. Each has an **Angle**, **Spacing**, **Length** and **Inset**. **Inset** is how far inside the edge the underlay stops, so it stays hidden.
- Open patterns (motifs, crosshatch) skip the automatic underlay, because it would show through the gaps.

Heavy fills on soft cloth benefit from two passes at different angles.

## Pull compensation

Thread pulls cloth inward, so stitched shapes come out smaller than you drew. **Pull compensation** makes the shape a little bigger on purpose.

![A column before and after pull compensation](diagrams/pull-compensation.svg)

- **Satin columns:** widens each side. 0.15 mm per side is the Standard starting value. Premium uses 0.20 mm. The slider goes up to 0.8 mm.
- **Fills:** grows the shape. The slider goes up to 1 mm.

Stretchy cloth pulls more. Lilo's Sewing setup raises compensation for knits to about 1.8 times the woven value.

### How to tell if you need more

Sew a test. If a 4 mm column measures 3.7 mm, or if the outline of a fill sits inside its border, raise pull compensation. If it looks fatter than your drawing or it overlaps its neighbours, lower it.

## Related

- [Satin tips](satin-tips.md)
- [Sewing setup](sewing-setup.md)
- [Fixing sew-out problems](sewout-troubleshooting.md)

pages.title: Satin tips
pages.summary: Choose a width, density and split for clean satin columns, and avoid the usual traps.
pages.body:
# Satin tips

A **satin column** is stitches that cross from one edge to the other. It looks smooth and shiny. It is the stitch behind most borders and letters.

![Satin column, with density and width marked](diagrams/satin-vs-fill.svg)

## Pick a width

- **Under 1.5 mm:** too thin. The stitches get tiny and can pile up. Use a **Triple** run instead.
- **2 to 6 mm:** the sweet spot.
- **Over 8 mm:** stitches get long and can snag. Lilo splits the column in two stitched halves, or you can use a fill.

## Density

**Density (spacing)** is the gap in millimetres between needle drops on the same side of the column. Smaller is denser.

- **0.40 mm** is the standard starting point for 40 wt thread.
- **0.35 mm** is about the tightest for 40 wt. Below that you risk thread breaks and holes.
- 60 wt thread needs a tighter gap, about 0.35 mm, because the thread is thinner.

The hint under the slider shows stitches per centimetre.

## Split above

**Split above** divides columns wider than this many millimetres into two halves, so no stitch is too long. Zero turns it off. Two controls appear when it is on:

- **Stagger cycles** repeats the pattern of the split line.
- **Stagger amount** shifts the split line sideways, so the join does not form a visible seam.

## Short stitches on curves

On the inside of a tight curve stitches bunch up. **Short stitches on curves** shortens some of them so the column stays even. Turn it on for curved borders and round letters.

## Underlay and pull compensation

Always use some underlay under a satin column wider than 1.5 mm. Read [Underlay and pull compensation](underlay-and-pull.md).

## Pick the stitch order

Sew a long satin column in one go, not as several short columns joined end to end. Lots of joins create thread jumps.

## Test first

Sew a 20 mm test strip at your chosen width and density on scrap cloth. Look for gaps (loosen less) and ridges or puckers (loosen more).

pages.title: Standard or Premium quality
pages.summary: What changes when you pick Premium, how many more stitches it makes and when it is worth it.
pages.body:
# Standard or Premium quality

**Quality** is one of three choices in the Sewing setup. It changes how carefully Lilo digitizes.

## Standard

- A fixed satin density of 0.40 mm.
- Underlay chosen by column width.
- Thin strokes become a single running line.
- Quick and predictable.

## Premium

- Spacing and pull compensation follow each column's width.
- Fine strokes sew as narrow satin, not as a faint line.
- Fills get edge walk and cross underlay.
- Columns that meet overlap slightly, so no gap shows.
- Tiny stitches are merged a little more aggressively (0.6 mm minimum instead of 0.5 mm).

## The cost

Premium usually makes about 1.2 to 1.6 times as many stitches as Standard. That means a longer sew. It varies by design.

## When to choose which

| Design | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| A logo with hairline serifs, like the Kadwood wordmark | Premium |
| A quick test, or a bold simple shape | Standard |
| Tiny text | Premium with 60 wt thread |
| A big fill with no fine detail | Standard |

## Changing quality later

Open the **Sewing setup** card and pick the other quality. Lilo updates shapes it made itself. It keeps anything you edited by hand. One undo step goes back.

## Related

[Sewing setup](sewing-setup.md), [Sewing setup presets](sewing-presets.md)

pages.body:
# Sewing setup

The **Sewing setup** card sits at the top of the right column. Its chip shows your current choice, like "Suiting, 40 wt, Standard". Click the chip to open it.

## Three choices

- **Fabric:** what you are sewing on. Suiting, shirting or lining, twill or caps, knit, denim, towel or leather.
- **Thread weight:** **40 wt** is standard. **60 wt** is fine, for small crisp detail.
- **Quality:** **Standard** or **Premium**. Read [Standard or Premium](standard-vs-premium.md).

Changing any of them updates the stitches Lilo made. Anything you edited by hand stays as you left it. One undo step reverses it.

## What the card also shows

The card lists what the setup calls for: needle, stabiliser, topping and hooping tips. The same list appears as **Before you sew** in the Export and Send windows, so you see it before you hit the machine.

![The Sewing setup card, open](screenshots/sewing-card.png)

## Stitch safety and speed

**Before you sew** also has a **Stitch safety** card and a suggested machine speed. Green means the setting sews well. Amber is a heads up, and the file still exports. Read [Stitch safety and machine speed](stitch-safety.md).

## Why it matters

A design for a thin suit lining sewn on a towel will sink and look thin. A design tuned for towel sewn on lining will pucker. The setup keeps the numbers matched to the cloth.

For a suit-lining monogram, choose **Shirting / lining**, **60 wt** if the letters are under 6 mm, and **Premium**.

## Every setup in detail

Read [Sewing setup presets](sewing-presets.md) for the full list of needles, stabilisers and tips for each fabric.

## It is a starting point

All numbers come from digitizing practice, not from a machine maker's rulebook. Always sew a test on scrap cloth first.

pages.title: Stitch safety and machine speed
pages.summary: The green and amber stitch ranges, what each amber note means, and the machine speed Lilo suggests.
pages.body:
# Stitch safety and machine speed

Some stitch settings sew well. Some make thread break or cloth pucker. Lilo shows you which is which, with a **green band** behind each slider.

Amber is a heads up. It is never a block. Lilo still makes the file and you can still export it.

## Where you see it

- **Before you sew:** open Export or Send and scroll to **Stitch safety**. It has one row for each setting your design uses.
- **On a shape:** select it. The sliders for spacing, stitch length, width and pull compensation carry the same green band.

![The Stitch safety card in Before you sew](screenshots/stitch-safety-card.png)

Inside the green, the dot is green. Outside it, the dot and the box turn amber and one short sentence says why. For example, a satin spacing of 0.30 mm says: "Too tight. The fabric puckers and the thread can break."

## Change many shapes at once

A slider in the **Stitch safety** card changes every shape of that kind. One undo puts them all back.

A satin shape's width is its drawing, so the card cannot widen it. Reshape it, or turn it into a running stitch.

## What will this change?

Under a slider you see how the change moved the design, like "+1,240 stitches · +1 min 30 s". It counts from where you started moving that slider. Lilo works it out in the background, so the screen stays smooth.

## The ranges

These are for 40 wt thread on cloth you wear. 60 wt and towel move a few numbers, noted below.

| Setting | Green range | Where the numbers come from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Satin width | 1.5 to 10 mm (60 wt: 1 to 10) | Lilo default. The 1.5 mm floor matches the calibration table. |
| Satin spacing | 0.35 to 0.60 mm (60 wt: from 0.30, towel: to 0.70) | Researched |
| Fill row spacing | 0.35 to 0.60 mm (60 wt: from 0.30) | Researched |
| Fill stitch length | 3 to 4.5 mm | Researched |
| Running stitch length | 1.5 to 4 mm (towel: to 5) | Lilo default |
| Pull compensation | 0.1 to 0.4 mm | Lilo default |
| Longest stitch | up to 7 mm on cloth you wear | Researched |

**Researched** means it comes from the sourced calibration table behind Lilo's defaults and from Brother and digitizing guides. **Lilo default** means it is Lilo's own choice, with no source behind it. Treat those as a good start, not a rule.

## Amber notes, in plain words

- **Satin too thin:** the column is narrower than the thread can cover. It will not look shiny. Use a running stitch, or switch to 60 wt thread.
- **Spacing too tight:** the cloth puckers and the thread can break.
- **Spacing too loose:** gaps. The cloth shows through.
- **Fill stitch too short:** the fill goes stiff and sews slowly.
- **Fill or running stitch too long:** it can snag on fingers and buttons.
- **Pull compensation too low:** edges may leave gaps. **Too high:** shapes come out fat.

Lilo also warns when a stitch is over 7 mm on cloth you wear. It still splits anything over 12.1 mm on its own. See [What the warnings mean](warnings-explained.md).

## Letters and thin lines

With 40 wt thread and Premium quality, custom-font letters now never use a satin column under 1.5 mm. Thinner strokes become a running stitch. A 1 mm column is too thin to look shiny, and it breaks thread. 60 wt thread still allows 1 mm.

## Machine speed

A file cannot set your machine's speed. You set it on the machine. Lilo suggests a speed for the design in **Before you sew**:

> Set your machine to **450** stitches a minute (thin lines in this design).

Lilo starts from the middle of the range for your fabric, then slows down for what is in the design.

| What is in the design | Suggested speed |
| --- | --- |
| Satin columns under 2 mm, or letters under 5 mm tall | 450 |
| Metallic thread | 400 |
| Very dense stitching | 550 |
| Leather, towel, denim | Their own slower range |

It never goes above the machine's top speed, 850 stitches a minute on the Brother NV2700. The caps are rules of thumb from Brother's FAQ and hobbyist guides. No maker publishes an exact table, so sew a test first.

On a Brother machine, look in Settings for **Max embroidery speed**. Menu names differ between models, so Lilo does not give exact steps.

## Sew time

**Before you sew** shows the time at 850 stitches a minute and the time at the suggested speed. The time counts:

- the stitches at that speed,
- 7 seconds for each thread cut,
- 45 seconds for each colour change,
- and a quarter extra for real life: checking, re-threading and the odd thread break.

The estimate is a guide. Your machine and your cloth decide.

# All fill patterns

This page is built from the app's own pattern list, so it always matches what you see in the picker. It has 36 patterns in three families.

- **Rows** are parallel lines of stitches. You can bend them, break them and fade them with a gradient.
- **Motif** patterns repeat a small shape across the area, like a brick or a weave.
- **Path** patterns follow the shape: rings, spirals, rays or flow lines.

Set the pattern in the **Fill pattern** section of the left panel. Each preview there shows the pattern on a 40 by 30 mm shape. Pull compensation, underlay and row spacing work the same for every pattern. Read about them in [Underlay and pull compensation](underlay-and-pull.md).

The classic fill: parallel rows with each row's stitches offset from its neighbours.

pages.title: Sewing setup presets
pages.summary: What each fabric, thread weight and quality choice means: needle, stabiliser, hooping and how the stitches change.
pages.body:
# Sewing setup presets

This page is built from the same tables the app uses for the **Sewing setup** card and the **Before you sew** checklist. Every number is a starting point. Sew a small test first, on a scrap of the same cloth.

You choose three things: the **fabric**, the **thread weight** and the **quality**. Lilo then picks stitch spacing, edge compensation and underlay for you. Read how they work in [Sewing setup](sewing-setup.md).

## Fabrics

### Suiting (woven wool / blends)

Jacket cloth and other firm wovens. It holds its shape, so it is the easy case.

- **Needle:** 75/11 sharp. A fresh sharp needle pierces the tight weave without pushing threads aside.
- **Stabiliser:** cut-away, medium, about 1.5-2 oz (50-60 g/m2). Cut-away keeps fine serifs from distorting as the garment is worn; trim close to the stitching.
- **Topping:** none needed.
- **Hooping:** Hoop the fabric together with the stabiliser, drum-tight but not stretched.
- **Hooping:** Do not clamp on a finished jacket front: float it on sticky stabiliser instead to avoid hoop marks.
- **What Lilo changes:** nothing. This is the baseline the other fabrics are measured against.

### Shirting / lining (light woven)

Thin cotton, silk or lining fabric. Puckers and shows needle holes easily, so lighter and looser.

- **Needle:** 70/10 sharp. Fine point so the holes stay small; 65/9 for the very thinnest silk.
- **Stabiliser:** no-show mesh, light, about 1 oz (30 g/m2). Soft mesh cut-away that will not show through or scratch; tear-away leaves holes along the stitching.
- **Topping:** none needed.
- **Hooping:** Hoop lightly: the fabric should lie flat, not be pulled.
- **Hooping:** Keep lining smooth, no ripples in the hoop.
- **What Lilo changes:** nothing. This is the baseline the other fabrics are measured against.

### Twill / caps

Cotton twill, chinos and structured caps. Stable, but heavier cloth swallows thin lines, so it wants more underlay.

- **Needle:** 75/11 sharp. 80/12 on thick caps or when the thread keeps shredding.
- **Stabiliser:** cut-away, medium, 2 oz (60 g/m2). For caps use a firm tear-away or cap backing and a cap frame.
- **Topping:** none needed.
- **Hooping:** Hoop twill drum-tight.
- **Hooping:** Caps: use the cap frame and make sure the seam is centred.
- **What Lilo changes:** line spacing is looser (x1.06).

### Knit / polo / jersey

Stretchy cloth. It moves under the needle, so it needs a firm backing, more edge compensation and solid underlay.

- **Needle:** 75/11 ballpoint. A ballpoint slides between the loops instead of cutting them.
- **Stabiliser:** cut-away, medium-heavy, 2.5 oz (75 g/m2). Always cut-away on knits; tear-away lets the design stretch out of shape in the wash.
- **Topping:** none needed.
- **Hooping:** Taut but never stretched: stretched knit springs back and puckers around the design.
- **Hooping:** A magnetic hoop holds knits without pulling them.
- **What Lilo changes:** edge compensation is 180 % of the woven value; line spacing is looser (x1.19); the narrowest satin column is 1.5 mm.

### Denim

Thick, tight cotton. Strong enough to take dense stitching, tough on small needles.

- **Needle:** 90/14 sharp. A jeans/denim needle (80/12 for lighter denim); a thin needle will deflect or snap.
- **Stabiliser:** cut-away, medium, 2 oz (60 g/m2). Tear-away is acceptable for heavy denim that does not stretch.
- **Topping:** none needed.
- **Hooping:** Hoop drum-tight; thick seams should not sit under the design.
- **What Lilo changes:** nothing. This is the baseline the other fabrics are measured against.

### Towel / terry / fleece

Pile fabric. Stitches sink into the loops, so fine lines vanish; use bolder shapes and a see-through topping.

- **Needle:** 75/11 sharp. 80/12 if the pile is deep.
- **Stabiliser:** tear-away, medium. Plus a layer of wash-away topping on top so the thread sits above the pile.
- **Topping:** a water-soluble topping on top, so the stitches do not sink into the pile.
- **Hooping:** Hoop the stabiliser and fabric together without crushing the pile.
- **Hooping:** Lay the water-soluble topping over the area before sewing and tear it away after.
- **What Lilo changes:** edge compensation is 150 % of the woven value; line spacing is looser (x1.6); the narrowest satin column is 2 mm.

### Leather / faux leather / vinyl

Every needle hole is permanent. Looser stitching and light underlay so it does not turn into a perforated line.

- **Needle:** 75/11 leather/wedge. A sharp or leather needle; not heavy-duty, to avoid big holes.
- **Stabiliser:** tear-away, medium. Tear-away only: cut-away backing makes the piece stiff and the cut edge can show.
- **Topping:** none needed.
- **Hooping:** Do not hoop leather, the hoop leaves a permanent ring: float it on sticky stabiliser and hold with clips or tape.
- **Hooping:** Test on an offcut: you cannot unpick without leaving holes.
- **What Lilo changes:** edge compensation is 80 % of the woven value; line spacing is looser (x1.3); the narrowest satin column is 1.5 mm; no zig-zag underlay.

## Thread weight

### 40 wt (standard)

The normal embroidery thread. Good cover on columns and fills; letters from about 6 mm tall; 60 wt from about 4 mm.

- **Needle:** 75/11 for most cloth (70/10 on lining).
- **Smallest letters:** 6 mm tall.

### 60 wt (fine)

Thinner thread for small, crisp detail. Satin density 0.35 mm instead of 0.40 (about 12 % closer) and finer columns are allowed. Do not swap it into a 40 wt file without redigitizing: coverage drops.

- **Needle:** 65/9 or 70/10 (75/11 on tougher cloth).
- **Smallest letters:** 4 mm tall.

## Quality

### Standard

The basic auto-digitize settings: a fixed 0.40 mm density and underlay by column width, thin strokes sewn as a single running line. Quick and predictable.

Typical stitch count: the baseline.

### Premium

Settings a professional digitizer would use: spacing and pull compensation follow each column's width, underlay is chosen by width, fine strokes become narrow satin instead of a faint line, fills get edge-walk and cross underlay, and columns that meet are trimmed so they overlap a hair instead of stacking.

Typical stitch count: about 1.3 times the Standard count.

pages.summary: Type a word or monogram, pick an embroidery font that suits the height, and add it to your design.

headings.text: A monogram for a suit lining

pages.body:
# Lettering: built-in fonts

Lilo comes with about a hundred **embroidery fonts**. These are not ordinary computer fonts. Each one was drawn to be sewn: the stitches follow the letter shape, and each font has a height range where it sews well.

## Add text

1. Choose the **Text** tool (press **T**) or **Type a monogram** on Home.
2. Click on the canvas where the text should go.
3. Type in the **Text** box in the left panel.
4. Choose a **Height (mm)**. Quick buttons give 6, 10, 15 and 25 mm. Or type your own.
5. Pick a font from the **Fonts** list.
6. Press **Add text**.

To change text later, select a word on the canvas. The panel becomes **Edit text**. Press **Update text** to apply your changes. **New text** starts another.

## The controls

- **Letter spacing** moves letters apart or closer together.
- **Line spacing** sets the gap between lines.
- **Align** is left, centre or right, for text with more than one line.
- The thread colour is the one in the panel's **Colour** control.

## Fit this height

Every font has a height range where it sews cleanly. The **Only fonts for N mm** checkbox hides fonts that do not suit your height. Leave it on while you choose.

A warning appears under the height box if the font is wrong for the size. For example, a font drawn for 15 to 30 mm letters piles up thread at 8 mm. Pick a font with a smaller range.

## A monogram for a suit lining

A 10 mm "JK" inside a suit jacket works well as follows.

1. Set the Sewing setup to **Shirting / lining**.
2. Choose a font that suits 10 mm with the checkbox on.
3. Use **Align: center** and add a little **Letter spacing**, about 0.5 mm.
4. Use a thread that is a shade off the lining, not a stark contrast.

## Small letters

Letters under about 6 mm with 40 wt thread fill in. Read [Small letters](small-letters.md).

## Your own fonts

Read [Using your own fonts](own-fonts.md).

## Licences

Every built-in font ships with its own licence. See [Licence and credits](licence-and-credits.md).

pages.title: Using your own fonts
pages.summary: Upload a TTF, OTF or TTC font and turn it into satin lettering.

headings.text: Choose a font that suits stitching

pages.body:
# Using your own fonts

You can add a font from your computer. This is how you stitch the exact typeface from a brand's logo.

## Upload

In the **Text** panel, scroll to **Your fonts** and press **Upload font (TTF, OTF, TTC)...**. Choose the file. Lilo adds it to the list. Press it to use it.

Press **Remove** next to a font to take it out.

## How it sews

An ordinary font has outlines, not stitches. Lilo converts each letter into **satin columns** that follow the shape of the strokes.

- Thick strokes become columns.
- Strokes that are too thin for a clean column are widened up to a minimum width.
- **Standard** quality sews columns no narrower than 1.5 mm. **Premium** allows 1.0 mm.

## Choose a font that suits stitching

- **Good:** sturdy sans-serif fonts and slab serifs, with strokes of even weight.
- **Tricky:** fonts with hairline strokes and heavy strokes together, like a high-contrast serif. The hairlines drop out.
- **Avoid:** very thin script fonts and fonts with tiny details.

## The small warning

If your font is too small to sew cleanly, a note says "Custom fonts sew best above N mm". Make the text taller or pick a built-in font.

## Licence

You are responsible for the licence of any font you upload. Lilo keeps the font on your computer.

## Related

[Small letters](small-letters.md), [Lettering: built-in fonts](lettering-fonts.md)

pages.title: Small letters
pages.summary: The smallest letters you can sew: 6 mm with 40 wt thread, 4 mm with 60 wt, and how to make small text sew clean.

headings.text: How to sew small text clean
Do not swap the thread without redigitizing
Letters on the inside of a jacket

pages.body:
# Small letters

Thread has thickness. Make letters small enough, and the thread fills the gaps inside the letters ("e" and "a" turn into blobs).

## The limits

| Thread | Smallest letter height |
| --- | --- |
| **40 wt** (standard) | **6 mm** |
| **60 wt** (fine) | **4 mm** |

**Height** here means the height of a capital letter.

Lilo checks this for every font. If your letters are shorter than the limit, a warning shows under the height box and in the warnings tray. It offers to switch to 60 wt thread.

## How to sew small text clean

1. Use **60 wt** thread. Change **Thread weight** in the Sewing setup. Then use a 65/9 or 70/10 needle.
2. Choose **Premium** quality. It spaces narrow columns a bit wider (0.45 mm) so they do not clog.
3. Pick a plain, sturdy font. Skip fonts with hairlines.
4. Use **cut-away** stabiliser. It gives the cleanest detail. Read [Embroidery basics](basics-materials.md).
5. Sew a test on scrap cloth first.

## Do not swap the thread without redigitizing

If you design for 40 wt and then put 60 wt thread on the machine, you lose coverage. Change **Thread weight** in the Sewing setup instead, so Lilo tightens the spacing.

## Letters on the inside of a jacket

A 5 mm "JK" on a shirt-weight lining: **Shirting / lining**, **60 wt**, **Premium**, a font that suits 5 mm. Expect the letters to shrink slightly in the wash and the pull of the thread.

## Related

[Lettering: built-in fonts](lettering-fonts.md), [What the warnings mean](warnings-explained.md)

pages.summary: Bend lettering round the top or bottom of a circle, for hat patches, badges and crests.

headings.text: Top and bottom text on one patch

pages.body:
# Text on a curve

Curved text is what you want round the edge of a hat patch or the rim of a crest. A name along the top of a 50 mm hat patch is a good example.

## Bend the text

1. Choose the **Text** tool (press **T**) and type your words.
2. Find **Curve** in the Text panel. It has three buttons:
   - **Straight** keeps the baseline flat. This is the default.
   - **Arc up** bends the words over the top of a circle. The letters stand on the outside.
   - **Arc down** bends them along the bottom of a circle. The letters stand on the inside, and still read left to right.
3. For a curve, a **Curve radius** slider appears. The radius is the size of the circle in millimetres. A smaller radius bends harder.
4. Press **Add text**.

A curve centres the words on the arc, so **Alignment** is ignored while a curve is on.

## Pick a radius

- The text should be shorter than the arc. A 30 mm radius gives an arc of about 150 mm. That is room for a name at 10 mm tall.
- For a round patch, make the radius a little smaller than the patch radius. A 50 mm patch is 25 mm from the centre, so try 20 mm and make the letters about 6 mm tall.
- If the text is too long for the circle, Lilo says so: "The text is N mm long but the path is only N mm". Make the radius bigger or the letters smaller.

## Change it later

Select the word. The panel becomes **Edit text** and the curve settings load into it. Change the buttons or the slider and press **Update text**. The word stays where you put it, and keeps any rotation you gave it. **⌘Z** undoes the change.

## Top and bottom text on one patch

Add the top words with **Arc up**. Then start new text with **New text**, and add the bottom words with **Arc down**. Move the second word until the two sit on the same circle. Use the **Measure** tool to check the gap.

## Related

[Lettering: built-in fonts](lettering-fonts.md), [Small letters](small-letters.md), [Sizing and hoops](sizing-and-hoops.md)

pages.title: Thread brands and matching
pages.summary: How Lilo picks real thread colours, how to change brands, and how colours reach your machine.

headings.text: Colours on screen are close, not exact

pages.body:
# Thread brands and matching

Embroidery thread comes in **brands** and **lines**. Each has its own colour names and codes. Lilo has a catalogue of tens of thousands of real thread colours across many brands.

## How matching works

Pictures have millions of colours. Thread has a few hundred per brand. When Lilo digitizes a picture, it finds the **nearest real thread** for each colour in the picture. It compares them the way the eye does, using a colour difference measure called CIEDE2000.

## Choose a brand

Before you digitize, use **Thread brand** in the **Auto digitize** panel. Pick the range you own or can buy. The number in brackets is how many colours it holds.

## Change a colour afterwards

1. Select a shape.
2. In the left panel, open **Colour**.
3. Search or browse the picker, then click a thread.

The picker lists the Brother, Country and Brothread ranges first. Every change is one undo step.

## Swap or merge colours

Open the **Colours** tab in the sequencer on the right.

- **Swap** replaces a thread with another everywhere it is used.
- **Merge into** folds one colour into another. Use it to cut down colour changes.
- **Select** selects every object in that colour.
- **Group by colour** reorders objects so each colour is sewn in one go.

Read [Fewer colour changes](fewer-colour-changes.md).

## Your own spools

**My Threads** keeps the spools you own. Tick **Use my threads** in Auto digitize to match to them first. Read [My Threads](my-threads.md).

## Colours in the machine file

Some file formats keep thread colours (PES, JEF, VP3, XXX). Others do not (DST, EXP, U01). Without colours, your machine shows "colour 1, colour 2". Read [File formats](formats-reference.md).

## Colours on screen are close, not exact

Screens cannot show thread exactly. A thread chart or the real spool is the final judge. Many brands have printed or online charts.

pages.title: My Threads
pages.summary: Keep a shelf of the spools you own, and make Lilo match pictures to them first.
pages.body:
# My Threads

**My Threads** is your shelf of real spools. Lilo uses it so its colours match what is in your drawer.

## Open it

In the sequencer on the right, open the **My Threads** tab.

## Add spools

Three ways:

1. **From the catalogue.** Type a brand, code or name into the search box and press **Add** next to the result. Adding the same spool again raises its quantity.
2. **By photo.** Read [Add a spool by photo](add-by-photo.md).
3. **By hand.** Fill in **Brand**, **Line**, **Code** and **Name** for a spool Lilo does not know.

## Look after the shelf

- Change the **Quantity** of each spool.
- Add **Notes**, like "half used" or "bought at the fair".
- **Remove** a spool when it is empty.

## Back up and move

- **Export JSON…** saves your shelf to a file.
- **Import JSON…** loads one back, on this or another computer.

If the shelf is empty on first open, you can restore a backup or **Start with an empty shelf**.

## Use it when digitizing

In **Auto digitize**, turn on **Use my threads**. Lilo matches the picture's colours to the spools on your shelf first. The panel says how many spools it is matching to. If the shelf is empty, it falls back to the brand you chose.

## Related

[Thread brands and matching](thread-brands-matching.md)

pages.title: Add a spool by photo
pages.summary: Photograph a thread label and let Lilo read it and suggest the thread.
pages.body:
# Add a spool by photo

You can add a spool without typing its code. Lilo reads the label from a photo.

## Steps

1. Open the **My Threads** tab in the sequencer.
2. Open **Add a spool by photo**.
3. Choose a photo of the label. Take it in good light, close enough to read the code, with no glare.
4. Lilo reads the text and suggests which thread it is.
5. **Check the suggestion.** Then confirm.

You always confirm. Lilo never adds a spool on its own.

## If Lilo reads it wrong

Reading text from a picture is not perfect. If the suggestion is wrong, search the catalogue by code, or fill in the spool by hand.

## Tips for a good photo

- Lay the spool on a plain surface.
- Hold the camera square to the label.
- Make sure the number and the brand name are both visible.
- Avoid shiny reflections on the plastic.

## Privacy

The photo is read on your computer. Lilo does not send it anywhere.

## Related

[My Threads](my-threads.md)

pages.title: The stitch player
pages.summary: Watch your design sew stitch by stitch, pause at colour changes, scrub to any point and read the totals.
pages.body:
# The stitch player

The **stitch player** is the bar under the canvas. It plays your design back the way the machine will sew it.

![The stitch player with a colour change card](screenshots/player.png)

## Controls

- **Play** and **Pause** start and stop the playback.
- **Scrub stitches** is the long slider. Drag it to jump to any point. Scrub to the start and press Play to watch from the beginning.
- **Speed** runs from 1 times to 50 times. At 1 times the on-screen needle moves as fast as a real machine, about 850 stitches a minute.
- **Auto-continue** waits a moment at each colour change and then carries on. Turn it off to stop at every one.

## Colour changes

When playback reaches a colour change it stops and shows a card: "Swap to Brother 123 and the thread name". It shows a swatch of the colour. Press **Continue** when you are ready. That is also how you will work at the machine: change the thread, then restart.

## The totals

The line under the bar tells you:

- **Stitches** so far out of the total.
- The number of **colour changes**.
- The design **size** in millimetres.
- An **estimated sewing time**, worked out at 850 stitches a minute.

## Why use it

- Spot a long jump that would leave a thread across the design.
- See whether the sewing order makes sense. Outlines sewn before fills can be covered up.
- Check the time. Add a few minutes per colour change for the thread swap.

Playing the design ticks the **Preview** step in the workflow strip.

## Related

[Realistic view](realistic-view.md), [The sequencer](sequencer.md)

pages.title: Realistic view and view options
pages.summary: Switch the canvas between a flat plan and a thread-like preview, and turn the grid, reference picture and jumps on or off.
pages.body:
# Realistic view and view options

The small checkboxes in the corner of the canvas change what you see. They never change the stitches.

## The four view options

- **Realistic** draws each stitch as a shaded thread, with heavier thread for triple, rope and satin. It shows how the design will really look.
- **Grid** shows a square grid on the canvas. Use it to line things up.
- **Reference** shows your original picture behind the stitches, so you can compare them.
- **Jumps** shows the thread that travels between shapes without sewing. These jumps are trimmed on the machine, but too many mean extra work.

Turn **Realistic** off to see a clean plan. It is easier to read when you are checking spacing.

## The hoop frame

You can also show the **hoop frame** with its clamp. Choose it in the **Hoop** section. It makes the preview look like the real hoop. Read [Sizing and hoops](sizing-and-hoops.md).

## Zoom and pan

- Scroll or pinch to zoom.
- Press **⌘K** and choose **Fit to window** to see the whole design.
- Hold **Space** and drag to pan.
- **Actual size** (⌘0) shows the true millimetre size on your screen.

## When to use which

| You want to | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Judge how it will look on a jacket | **Realistic**, zoomed in |
| Find holes between shapes | **Realistic** off |
| Compare against the original logo | **Reference** on |
| Cut thread trims | **Jumps** on |

Switching **Realistic** counts as a look at the preview, so it ticks the **Preview** step.

## Related

[The stitch player](stitch-player.md)

pages.title: The sequencer
pages.summary: Change the order shapes are sewn in, hide shapes, group by colour, and manage reference images.
pages.body:
# The sequencer

The **sequencer** is the panel on the right. It lists your shapes in the order the machine will sew them. It has four tabs.

## Objects

Each row is a shape. Rows are grouped into **colour blocks**. A colour block is a run of shapes that use the same thread, so the machine does not change thread inside it.

- **Move up** and **Move down** change the sewing order.
- **Hide** takes a shape off the canvas and out of the file. Use it to check one layer at a time.
- Double-click a name to **rename** it.
- **Details** shows stitch and point counts.
- Each colour block can move up or down as a whole.

### Order matters

Sew big fills first, then borders, then details on top. If a fill is sewn after its outline, the fill covers it.

## Colours

The **Colours** tab lists each thread and how many objects and stitches use it.

- **Group by colour** reorders objects so each colour is sewn once. It cuts thread changes.
- **Merge into** folds a colour into another.
- **Swap** replaces a thread with a different one.
- **Select** selects every object of that colour.

Read [Fewer colour changes](fewer-colour-changes.md).

## Images

The **Images** tab holds reference pictures. They are not stitched.

- **Add image…** puts a picture behind the design to trace over or compare to.
- Set the **opacity** and **width**.
- **Lock** so you cannot drag it by accident. **Hide** and **Remove** work as you expect.

## My Threads

The fourth tab is your shelf of spools. Read [My Threads](my-threads.md).

## Related

[The stitch player](stitch-player.md)

pages.title: Fewer colour changes
pages.summary: Why each thread swap costs time, and four ways to cut them.

headings.text: 1. Use fewer colours when you digitize

pages.body:
# Fewer colour changes

A single-needle home machine stops at every colour change. You swap the thread by hand, thread the needle and restart. A design with 12 colour changes can take longer to swap than to sew.

The stitch player counts them, and the warnings tray tells you when there are many.

## Four ways to cut them

### 1. Use fewer colours when you digitize

In **Auto digitize**, lower **Colours**. A logo that looks fine with 4 colours does not need 8.

### 2. Merge similar colours

Open the **Colours** tab in the sequencer. Pick **Merge into** on a colour that is close to another. Every shape in the first colour joins the second.

### 3. Group by colour

If the same thread is used in several places, the machine may swap away and back. Press **Group by colour** in the **Colours** tab. Lilo reorders the objects so each colour is sewn in one block.

Check the new order in the stitch player. Sewing order affects what covers what.

### 4. Reuse a thread

Use one thread for two roles. For a garment-bag crest, sew the outline and the lettering in the same gold. That is one swap saved.

## What counts as many

Lilo's tray suggests a look at your colours when a design has more than 8 colour changes. That is a guide, not a rule. A rich crest may need more.

## Related

[Thread brands and matching](thread-brands-matching.md), [The sequencer](sequencer.md)

pages.title: Set up Wi-Fi sending with Lilo Link
pages.summary: Connect a Brother or Baby Lock machine to your Wi-Fi so Lilo can find it and send designs.

headings.text: Windows and Linux: check the firewall

pages.body:
# Set up Wi-Fi sending with Lilo Link

**Lilo Link** is the part of Lilo that talks to your sewing machine over Wi-Fi. It works with **Brother** and **Baby Lock** machines that have Wi-Fi built in. Other machines use a [USB stick](usb-stick.md).

## Before you start

- **Your machine must have Wi-Fi.** Look for a Wi-Fi symbol on the screen or the box.
- **Use a 2.4 GHz network.** Most embroidery machines cannot join a 5 GHz network. If your router has one name for both, connect the machine to the 2.4 GHz band. If you have two separate names, pick the one that ends in "2.4" or has no "5G".
- **Put your computer and your machine on the same network.** Not a guest network. Not a separate office Wi-Fi. If they are on different networks, Lilo cannot see the machine.

## Connect the machine

1. On the machine, open its **Wi-Fi settings** and join your 2.4 GHz network. Follow the machine's own manual for this part.
2. Check that the machine shows it is connected.

## Find it in Lilo

1. Open **Lilo Link** from the top of the window. Go to **Machines**.
2. Press **Scan network**. Lilo looks across your local network and lists what it finds under **Discovered on the network**.
3. Press **Save** next to your machine. It moves to **Saved machines**.
4. Press **Test** to check the connection.

Lilo detects the machine on its own. You do not need to type an address. If the scan finds nothing, you can type the machine's IP address under **Add machine manually**. The machine shows its IP address in its Wi-Fi or network screen.

## Mac: allow Local Network

The first time you scan, macOS asks to allow **Local Network** access. Choose **Allow**. If you said no by mistake, go to **System Settings, Privacy and Security, Local Network** and switch Lilo on.

## Windows and Linux: check the firewall

If scanning finds nothing and everything else is right, a firewall or security program may be blocking Lilo. Allow Lilo on your home (private) network.

## Next step

Read [Send a design](send-a-design.md). If something goes wrong, read [Wi-Fi troubleshooting](send-troubleshooting.md).
